newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian police accuse cinema managers of homicide.
newsitem.headline: Indian police accuse cinema managers of homicide.

text.p: Indian police on Saturday accused four cinema managers of homicide after a fire in a New Delhi movie theatre killed 57 people.

A Delhi judge denied bail to the four men and remanded them to police custody for 14 days while investigators probe the causes of Friday's blaze in the packed Uphaar Grand movie theatre in the capital.

"They have been accused of culpable homocide not amounting to murder," the managers' lawyer, Kewal Krishan Sareen, told Reuters after the four were arraigned in court. The charges carry a maximum punishment of 14 years in jail.
Sareen said the four accused would lodge an appeal with another court to try to win bail.

Deputy police commissioner Maxwell Perreira said more people were expected to be detained following the fire in the basement of the cinema which sent toxic smoke into the theatre, triggering a stampede and suffocating most of the victims.
"More arrests are likely," Perreira told Reuters.

Perreira said a small fire had broken out on Friday morning in an electrical transformer which hours later exploded in flames during the premiere of the new Hindi movie "Border", which dramatises a 1971 battle between India and Pakistan.
"We will have to see to what extent the transformer was repaired," the police official said.

The company which owns the cinema, Ansal Properties, confirmed there was a small fire in the transformer in the morning, but said the city's electricity board had assured the managers that it had been repaired and was safe.
"There is absolutely no criminal negligence on our side," Ansal spokesman R. Gurumoorthy told Reuters. Officials of the Delhi electricity board could not be reached for comment.
Sareen said there were two transformers on the cinema's premises, one for the theatre and the other for the neighbourhood.
"The tranformer that tripped was the one under the control of the Delhi electricity authorities," Sareen said. "So how can we be accused of negligence?"
Perreira said most of the victims were trapped in the balcony and suffocated when poisonous smoke engulfed the theatre, which was packed to its capacity of 1,050 seats.
He said the death toll, which late on Friday had been set at 58, had been revised down to 57. A police spokesman said 91 people were injured.
The transformer was in the basement of the 24-year-old cinema in an affluent South Delhi neighbourhood.
"It generated tremendous heat in the entire cable system and the sound-proofing in the walls, which had combustible material, began to smoulder," Perreira said.
"Smoke began collecting in any available space, and by the time the fire broke out, all the escape routes were blocked."
Witnesses described horrific scenes. "I saw women with children in their arms breaking windows and jumping out. It was unbelievable," said one.
"People in the balcony tried to rush into the toilets. The doors to the exits first would not open, and when they did, billowing smoke poured through," Perreira said.
Fire authorities had recently inspected the cinema and certified that it satisfied safety regulations, Perreira said.
